column4: This ayah itself sets two arrivals side by side: a covering punishment (غاشية) may come to them, or the Hour may come suddenly; it exactly unfolds the section's reading of 88:1.
Each community has a direction (وجهة) toward which it turns, yet wherever people are God will bring them all together; chosen orientation and unavoidable arrival meet in one ayah.
The death from which people flee will meet them, after which they are returned to the Knower and informed of their deeds; turning away cannot alter arrival, return, or reckoning.
The Messenger's charge is only delivery while the reckoning belongs to God, precisely matching the movement from “you are only a reminder” to “upon Us is their account.”
The Prophet is told not to grieve at disbelief: “to Us is their return,” and God will then inform them of what they did, reproducing the section's sequence and stance.
After 31:23's return, this ayah gives the brief worldly enjoyment followed by being driven into severe punishment; it shows the steps concealed between turning away and the final destination.
Clear messengers came to earlier peoples, but they disbelieved and turned away (كَفَرُوا وَتَوَلَّوا); arrival of warning and the response of 88:23 are joined directly.
The turners of 64:6 deny resurrection, but are told they will certainly be raised and informed of their deeds; this completes their unavoidable return and account.
Moses and Aaron are told that punishment falls on whoever denies and turns away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى), the exact moral pair behind 88:23-24.
The nearer punishment is distinguished from the greater punishment so that people may return; it makes explicit the section's claim that return remains voluntary before the final punishment.
Humanity's reckoning has drawn near while they remain heedlessly turning away; impending account and present aversion are compressed into one sentence.
“To your Lord that day is the driving” makes the destination unavoidable immediately before the passage describes the person who denied and turned away.
The person “denied and turned away” (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى), echoing 88:23, within a scene whose stated destination is the Lord in 75:30.
Every human is laboring step by step toward the Lord and will meet Him; this directly renders the section's claim that even apparent departure is movement toward return.
The doomed person thought he would never return (أَن لَّن يَحُورَ), exposing as delusion the belief that turning one's back changes the destination.
One who breaks with the Messenger is turned toward what he chose (نُوَلِّهِ مَا تَوَلَّى) and brought to Hell; chosen orientation becomes final destination.
The blaze calls the one who turned his back and turned away (أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّى); the fugitive gesture itself cannot keep punishment from summoning him.
Wherever people turn (تُوَلُّوا), there is God's face; the directional sense of the root shows spatial turning cannot place anyone outside the divine relation.
The command to set one's face toward the upright religion comes before a day arrives from God that cannot be turned back; voluntary orientation precedes irreversible arrival.
People are commanded to turn penitently to their Lord and submit before punishment comes; this is the voluntary return the section sets against compulsory return.
Paradise is what was promised to every أَوَّاب, one repeatedly returning, and guardian; the named voluntary branch of the root is attached to its good destination.
Hell is “a place of return” (مَآبًا) for the transgressors, supplying the first of the section's two opposed destinations.
On the true Day, whoever wills may take toward the Lord a مَآبًا; the same return noun becomes a voluntarily chosen way rather than the transgressors' destination in 78:22.
The tranquil soul is told to return to its Lord content and pleasing; this directly joins voluntary return to the satisfaction evoked by 88:9.
After the human deems himself self-sufficient and transgresses, this ayah answers that the return is to the Lord, so imagined independence cannot change the endpoint.
God gives life and death and “to Us is the destination”; the first-person divine destination directly parallels “to Us is their return.”
Worldly enjoyment is followed by return to God and severe punishment for disbelief, closely matching the little enjoyment, return, and punishment sequence developed in the prose.
The ayah addresses disbelief and gratitude, then says the return is to the Lord and He will inform people of what they did; response, return, and account remain linked.
Every being in the heavens and earth comes to the Merciful as a servant; universal coming strips away every claimed escape or independence.
Between universal servanthood in 19:93 and each person's solitary coming in 19:95, God has counted every one exactly, joining return to reckoning.
Every one of them will come to Him individually on Resurrection Day, a direct scene of the inevitable arrival implied by إِيَابَهُمْ.
Whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal encounters Hell, giving the evil side of the section's statement that coming may bear good or evil.
Whoever comes to Him as a believer with righteous deeds receives the highest ranks, completing the opposed good arrival begun in 20:74.
Whoever comes with a good deed receives better and is safe from that Day's terror; moral content and the manner of arrival are directly joined.
Whoever comes with an evil deed is cast face-first into the Fire; it supplies the evil arrival and also makes the face bear its outcome.
Righteousness is not the mere turning of faces east or west; the ayah marks the boundary between physical orientation and the moral turning at issue in 88:23.

God observes the Prophet's face turning toward heaven and appoints a pleasing direction, repeatedly commanding him to turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque; face and turning function as literal orientation.
The question “what turned them from their direction?” uses the same turning root for a change of qiblah, clarifying the spatial branch beside moral turning away.
A clarifying messenger had already come to them, establishing the arrival to which their turning in the next ayah responds.
After the messenger's coming in 44:13, they turn away from him and accuse him; it stages arrival followed immediately by aversion.
Whenever a sign from their Lord comes to them, they turn away from it; coming and abandonment of nearness form the repeated action.
This repeated formulation says no sign from their Lord comes without their turning away, again joining arrival to deliberate aversion.
Every renewed reminder that comes from the Merciful finds them turning away from it, directly coupling the coming reminder with the response in 88:23.
Whoever turns away is outside the Messenger's charge, for he was not sent as their keeper; this closely matches reminder without control in 88:21-23.
The Prophet is not a compeller over them and must remind by the Quran whoever fears the warning; it is a near-parallel to 88:21-22 and its receptive addressee.
The command to remind when reminder benefits supplies the same prophetic act that immediately precedes the turning away in surah 88.
The person who fears will take the reminder, identifying the responsive hearer of the command in 87:9 and contrasting the one who turns away.
If they turn away, the Prophet was not sent as their guardian and is charged only with delivery; the same response and limit on prophetic control are explicit.
If people turn away, the Messenger bears only his assigned duty and his obligation is clear delivery; it parallels the reminder's bounded responsibility.
Obedience is commanded, but if people turn away the Messenger's task is only clear delivery; freedom to turn and responsibility for it remain distinct.
If they turn away, the Messenger's task is only clear delivery, matching the stance from which 88:21 addresses the Prophet.
After asking whether they will submit, the ayah says that if they turn away the Messenger's duty is only delivery; direction of response is left to the hearers.
Hud says he has delivered the message; if they turn away, God can replace them and they cannot harm Him, showing their turning changes neither the message nor divine power.
Abraham's prayer holds voluntary turning and final destination together: “to You we have turned” and “to You is the destination.”
Every soul tastes death, people are tested by evil and good, and to God they are returned; both kinds of coming experience terminate in the same return.
All people's return is to God, who will inform them of what they did; the ayah directly binds return to disclosed deeds.
Each soul bears its own earning, then all return to their Lord and are informed of their disputes; individual responsibility culminates in return and account.
God knows people's present position and, on the day they are returned to Him, will inform them of their deeds; no orientation is hidden from the final disclosure.
People are told to act because God, the Messenger, and believers will see, after which they are returned to the Knower and informed of their deeds.
Some faces on that Day are radiant, beginning a two-sided face scene parallel to the two groups of faces in surah 88.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord, making the blessed face's orientation explicit.
Other faces on that Day are grim, opening the opposed facial condition just as 88:2 stands against 88:8.
The grim faces expect a crushing calamity, connecting the visible face to its anticipated end.
Faces on that Day are bright, beginning another direct counterpart to surah 88's contrasting faces.
Their laughing and rejoicing completes the blessed face's visible condition.
Other faces on that Day bear dust, introducing the opposite group.
Darkness covers those faces, joining the face contrast to the image of covering.
Those who do good receive the best, and neither darkness nor humiliation covers their faces; the negated covering defines the blessed side of the image.
Those who earn evil are covered with humiliation, and their faces seem covered by pieces of dark night; face, covering, and outcome meet directly.
Fire covers their faces, combining the section's face with the punitive sense of an overwhelming covering.
The commanded watch is for a day when heaven comes with visible smoke, supplying the arrival in a two-ayah covering scene.
The smoke of 44:10 covers the people and is named a painful punishment, showing a coming thing becoming an enveloping affliction.
Punishment covers them from above and from beneath their feet, a direct punitive realization of the covering image.
They await only the Hour coming suddenly while they do not perceive, closely repeating the sudden-arrival half of 12:107.
They await only the Hour to come suddenly, although its signs have already come; anticipated arrival and prior arrivals are juxtaposed.
Disbelievers remain in doubt until the Hour comes suddenly or the punishment of a barren day comes, giving two feared arrivals.
Punishment comes to them suddenly while they do not perceive, preserving both unforeseen arrival and lack of awareness.
The hastened punishment has an appointed time and will surely come suddenly while they do not perceive.
Following revelation is urged before punishment comes suddenly and unnoticed, continuing the opportunity for voluntary return in 39:54.
The Hour will come only suddenly; its hidden timing intensifies the section's sense of an arrival that cannot be managed by the one it reaches.
The threatened event comes suddenly, confounds them, and cannot be repelled or delayed; its arrival removes every avenue of evasion.
“Has the account of Moses come to you?” repeats the precise construction in which a report is represented as arriving to its hearer.
The same question about Moses' report coming to the Prophet confirms the section's reading of أَتَىٰكَ as the arrival of news.
The report of Abraham's honored guests is asked as something that has come to the Prophet, another direct instance of news arriving.
The report of the hosts is likewise phrased as having come to the Prophet, repeating the verbal scene of 88:1.
The news of the disputants is asked as something that has come to the Prophet, extending the “arriving report” formula from حديث to نبأ.
God knows the inner self and is forgiving to the أَوَّابِين, those who repeatedly return; voluntary return is grounded in inward rectitude and forgiveness.
David is described as أَوَّاب, ever returning; the named root becomes a sustained quality of a servant rather than only the final return of all people.
Solomon is praised as an excellent servant, أَوَّاب, repeating voluntary return as the defining quality of a prophet.
Job too is praised as an excellent servant, أَوَّاب, showing steadfast return through trial.
After listing the attractions of the nearer life, the ayah says that with God is the good مَآب; worldly objects are set against the enduring return-place.
Those who believe and do right have joy and a good مَآب, explicitly naming the favorable return-place.
The Prophet says he was commanded to worship God, calls to Him, and that to Him is his مَآب; mission, direction, and return share one endpoint.
David has nearness with God and a good مَآب, attaching the return-place to restored closeness after repentance.
Solomon has nearness with God and a good مَآب, again joining voluntary return to its favorable end.
The righteous are promised a good مَآب, stating one side of the opposed return-places developed in the section.
The transgressors have an evil مَآب, reversing 38:49 with the same noun and clarifying that everyone returns but not to the same reception.
The person given his record in his right hand receives an easy account; after the meeting in 84:6, the return proceeds to precisely the reckoning named in 88:26.
The Prophet has none of his followers' account upon him, nor they his; it marks the boundary that explains why account belongs to God rather than the reminder.
Noah says his followers' account rests only with his Lord, a direct prophetic statement of the division of responsibility found at the close of surah 88.
Pharaoh and his forces act arrogantly and suppose they will not be returned to God, voicing the false premise behind turning away.
God seizes and casts them into the sea, overturning the supposition of 28:39 with an inescapable divine seizure.
The ungrateful person doubts the Hour, imagines a favorable return, but is promised disclosure of deeds and severe punishment; false confidence cannot cancel return or account.
When favored, the human turns away and withdraws to his side; beside 41:50 it connects the bodily gesture of abandoning nearness to mistaken ideas about return.
People are told to seek forgiveness and return penitently for good provision; if they turn away, a great day's punishment is feared, setting the two orientations against each other.
Hud commands repentance and asks his people not to turn away as criminals; voluntary return and culpable departure are made explicit alternatives.
Affliction makes a person call on the Lord while turning penitently to Him, but relief is followed by forgetting and disbelief; the ayah exposes unstable, reversible orientation.
When death comes, the wrongdoer asks to be returned, locating the wish for voluntary amendment only after its opportunity has ended.
The requested return is refused and a barrier remains until resurrection; compulsory forward movement replaces the return the person delayed.
Criminals before their Lord ask to be sent back so they can act rightly; their belated request contrasts with the still-open return sought by the lesser punishment in 32:21.
Standing before the Fire, they wish to be returned so they will no longer deny; arrival at punishment produces a return that is only a wish.
God states that if they were returned they would resume what they were forbidden, revealing that mere reversal of location would not be genuine return to God.
On that Day the settled destination (ٱلْمُسْتَقَرُّ) is to the Lord, closely matching the dictionary description of return to one's place of settlement.
The human asks “where is the escape?” on Resurrection Day, exposing the impulse to flee just before 75:12 names the settled destination.
The answer “no refuge” closes off evasion and prepares the declaration that the destination is the Lord.
The final endpoint is to the Lord; this nonlexical formulation states why neither facing nor turning away can alter where movement ends.
People are told to walk through the earth and eat God's provision, but to Him is the resurrection; ordinary movement across the world terminates in return.
A single blast brings everyone together, present before God; the universal arrival is immediate and collective.
After the gathering in 36:53, no soul is wronged and all are repaid for deeds, completing arrival with account.
Every soul comes accompanied by a driver and witness, staging the compulsory arrival that turns into judgment.
Only the one who comes to God with a sound heart is saved; the quality of the voluntary coming determines the reception at the common destination.
The promised person fears the Merciful unseen and comes with a penitent heart, combining chosen inward return with actual arrival.
The Prophet himself turns away from the blind visitor and is corrected; this bounds the root's moral force, since the gesture is not disbelief yet still carries responsibility.
Those whom God lets stray have no protector and, on seeing punishment, ask whether there is any way of return; the possible return of life has become impossible.
At punishment a soul wishes for another return so it might do good; this belated “return” defines the deadline implicit in the command of 39:54.
When punishment comes, wrongdoers ask for a short delay so they may answer the call and follow messengers; arrival makes the formerly voluntary response unavailable.
The sudden cry leaves no time even for a bequest or return to one's family; earthly return to a familiar settlement is barred as final return begins.
A destroyed town cannot return to earthly life, distinguishing the denied worldly return from the universal return to God.
The one who enters the blazing fire is defined as the person who denied and turned away; its exact phrase mirrors 88:23 and fixes the consequence.
The warning of a blazing fire supplies the punishment into which the denier who turns away in 92:16 enters.
The other recipient is given his record from behind his back; the turned back becomes the place where the evidence of account reaches him.
The answer to his belief that he would not return is that his Lord always saw him, so denial of return never removed him from divine sight.
The person who worships on an edge reverses course on his face when trial comes; bodily orientation images a conditional commitment that fails under hardship.
Repentance is offered as good, but those who turn away are told they cannot frustrate God; their chosen departure cannot produce escape.
Hypocrites are told to “go back” and seek light, but a wall is then set between them and the believers; the commanded return exposes that the earlier opportunity has passed.
One who submits his face to God and does good has reward and security; willing face-direction supplies the positive reverse of turning away.
Submitting one's face to God while doing good is grasping the firmest handhold; chosen orientation creates nearness rather than abandoning it.
The best religion belongs to one who submits his face to God and does good, a positive orientation opposed to the face and back of refusal.
The repeated command to turn the face toward the Sacred Mosque confirms that وَجْه and the turning root can jointly describe concrete direction.
The qiblah command is extended to every location: all are to turn their faces toward it, a collective use of orientation distinct from rejection.
Abraham says he has directed his face toward the Creator of heavens and earth; the face serves as an image of wholehearted chosen orientation.
The Prophet is commanded to set his face to the religion as a monotheist, making face-direction a continuing religious stance.
Setting the face toward the upright religion turns a spatial image into stable moral orientation.
On the Day when some faces whiten and others blacken, the face visibly registers two opposed outcomes, as it does in surah 88.
Those whose faces whiten abide in God's mercy, completing the favorable half of the face contrast in 3:106.
Faces are humbled before the Living, Self-Sustaining One; their Day-of-Judgment orientation conveys the submission that cannot then be refused.
Those who lied about God are seen on Resurrection Day with darkened faces, letting disbelief appear in the face at the destination.
Those exposed to the Fire are humbled by abasement and look furtively, a final posture of those who lost themselves.
When the promised event is seen near, the disbelievers' faces become distressed; arrival is registered visibly on the face.
Night “when it covers” supplies the plain enveloping sense of the root غ ش و that the section sets beside its idiom of coming.
What covers the lote tree covers it, another pure covering use that helps preserve the distinction behind the section's coming gloss.
God's command is spoken of as already having come and people are told not to hasten it; prophetic perfect makes the future arrival certain.
The ayah asks whether they await the angels, the Lord, or signs of the Lord to come, then warns that belief at that arrival will no longer benefit.
The wrongdoers await only the angels or their Lord's command to come; arrival marks the end of their present choice.
Those who hold back are asked whether they await God and the angels coming and the matter being decided; decisive arrival closes deliberation.
People offer excuses when the believers return to them, but they will themselves be returned to the Knower and informed of their deeds; a small return anticipates the final one.
God knows what people earn, raises them by day until the term is fulfilled, then to Him is their return and disclosure; daily return rehearses final return.
Whether the Prophet sees part of the threat or dies first, the opponents' return is to God, who witnesses their deeds; prophetic timing does not affect their destination.
Whether the Messenger is shown part of the promise or taken in death, the opponents will be returned to God; the outcome does not depend on what the Prophet witnesses.
The Prophet receives the Book for humanity; guidance or error belongs to each person and he is not their trustee, clarifying noncoercive reminder.
The truth has come from the Lord; each person's guidance or error is his own, and the Prophet is not their keeper, linking arrival of truth to free response.
God guides to Himself whoever turns penitently, stating the voluntary divineward movement that the section derives from أَوَّاب.
God chooses and guides to Himself the one who turns penitently; willing return is presented as a path of guidance.
Created signs are an insight and reminder for every penitent servant, joining reminder's efficacy to an already returning orientation.
Abraham comes to his Lord with a sound heart; like 26:89, the arrival is inwardly prepared rather than merely compulsory.
Coming with a good deed or an evil deed produces distinct recompense, a broad counterpart to the lexicon's good and evil sides of coming.
The one who comes with good receives better, while the one who comes with evil receives only what was done; arrival issues directly in account.
God gives life, causes death, and then gathers everyone on the unquestionable Day; life's movement is gathered into a single return.
People issue forth in separate groups to be shown their deeds, a scene in which final movement culminates in disclosure.
Even an atom's weight of good is seen, specifying the exactness of the account reached in 99:6.
Even an atom's weight of evil is seen, completing the two-sided precision of that account.
The gathered birds are described with the return root in relation to David; this responsive recurring movement is a distinct concrete shade of ء و ب.
Mountains and birds are commanded to echo or repeatedly turn with David (أَوِّبِي), preserving the root's sense of responsive recurrence beyond human repentance.
Pharaoh turns away, gathers his scheme, and then comes; literal departure followed by arrival makes the two motion verbs visible without yet naming final return.
Pharaoh turns away with his supporting power and dismisses Moses, a political and bodily enactment of abandoning the messenger's nearness.
When favored, the human turns away and withdraws to his side; the posture supplies the bodily scene underlying moral refusal.
The Prophet is told to turn from the one who has turned from God's reminder and desires only the nearer life; reciprocal distance follows the hearer's first refusal.
